Webflow is a website platform where you design visually but the result is real HTML, CSS and JavaScript. When you drag a box onto the canvas and give it padding, Webflow writes the CSS rule for you. That is the big difference from simple drag-and-drop builders: in Webflow you are working with the same building blocks a front-end developer types by hand, so you need to understand them. This course assumes you already use a computer comfortably and have built at least a simple page somewhere before.

The three parts you will use every day

**The Designer**: the visual workspace where you build pages, set styles, make layouts responsive and add interactions. It runs in a desktop browser such as Chrome. It is not built for phones, so plan to work on a laptop.

**The CMS (Content Management System)**: databases called Collections, for content that repeats in the same shape, such as blog posts, menu items, properties or team members. Clients can add items without touching your design.
**Hosting**: Webflow serves the finished site. Every project gets a free staging address ending in webflow.io. Connecting a real domain such as yourbusiness.com.ng needs a paid Site plan.
Workspace plans and Site plans

Webflow charges in two separate ways, and clients often confuse them. A **Workspace plan** is for you, the builder: it controls how many projects you can keep, whether you can export code, and how many people can work with you. A **Site plan** is for each live website: it controls the custom domain, CMS item limits, form submissions and traffic. A common professional setup is that you hold a Workspace plan, build the site, then the client pays for their own Site plan so the website is legally and financially theirs. Prices are set in US dollars and change from time to time, so always check webflow.com/pricing on the day you quote.
Dollar billing in Nigeria

Webflow bills by card in US dollars. Many Nigerian bank cards have limits on foreign currency spending that change often. Before you promise a launch date, confirm that you or the client has a card that can make the payment, for example a dollar card from a bank or fintech app. Never pay a client's hosting with your own card without a written agreement on repayment.

The box model, page structure and class naming
Explain content, padding, border and margin and calculate an element's total width

Every element on a web page is a rectangle. A heading, a button, an image and the box that holds them are all boxes. The **box model** describes the layers of each box, from the inside out: the **content**, then **padding** (space inside the edge), then the **border**, then **margin** (space outside the edge, pushing other boxes away). In Webflow's Style panel you will find these under Spacing and Borders. If you understand these four layers, most layout problems stop being mysterious.
Designer arranging interface blocks and components
Every element is a box, and pages are boxes nested inside boxes.
Worked example: why the card is too wide
For example, Tolu sets a service card to width 300px, padding 24px on each side and a 1px border. Three cards in a row with 20px gaps overflow her 960px container.
With the default box sizing called content-box, width means the content only. Total card width = 300 + 24 + 24 + 1 + 1 = 350px.
Three cards and two gaps: 350 x 3 + 20 x 2 = 1,050 + 40 = 1,090px, which is 130px wider than 960px.
Webflow's default styles set box-sizing to border-box, where width includes padding and border. With border-box the card is exactly 300px, so the row is 300 x 3 + 40 = 940px and fits.
Tolu checks the Style panel and finds an old custom code embed that changed box-sizing. She removes it and the row fits.
Knowing which box-sizing applies tells you how to add widths correctly: 940px fits inside 960px, 1,090px does not.
A clean page structure

Professional Webflow builds follow a predictable nesting pattern. Open the **Navigator** panel and you should see a tidy tree, not a pile of unnamed Div Blocks. A common pattern is: Body, then a **Section** for each band of the page (hero, services, testimonials, footer), then a **Container** that limits the width and centres the content, then Div Blocks, Grids or Flex boxes for the layout, then the text, images and buttons.

Each level has one job, so you can change spacing or width in one place without breaking the rest.
**Section** sets top and bottom padding and the background colour of a band.
**Container** sets a maximum width, for example 1200px, and centres it with automatic left and right margins.
**Layout wrapper** decides how children sit: side by side (flex), in a grid, or stacked.
**Content elements** carry typography and images. Use real headings (H1 to H6) in order, not paragraphs made big.
Classes, combo classes and why they matter

In Webflow you style elements by giving them a **class**, which is a reusable named style. Give five buttons the class button and change its colour once: all five update. A **combo class** adds a variation on top of a base class, for example button plus is-secondary for an outline version. The base styles stay shared; only the differences live in the combo class. If you instead style each button separately, you create dozens of near-identical classes and the site becomes painful to change.
Global styles first

Before building any section, style the tags themselves: Body (font, size, colour), H1 to H6, Paragraph, Links and lists. Select the element, then choose the tag in the selector field rather than adding a class. Every new element then looks right by default, and you only add classes for real differences.
A naming system you can hand to a client

Names should tell the next person what an element is. Many Webflow professionals use **Client-First**, a free naming convention published by Finsweet. In Client-First, custom classes describe the component and the element with an underscore, such as header_component or services_card, while utility classes describe one job, such as padding-section-large or text-align-center. Whether you adopt Client-First fully or not, pick one system and use it for the whole project.

Clean structure is not just tidiness. A clear Navigator tree makes responsive fixes faster, keeps the CSS file smaller (which helps loading speed), and lets the client or another developer find things months later. Fix the most common mobile layout problems

Most visitors to a Nigerian small business website arrive on a phone, often over mobile data. A layout that looks perfect on your laptop but breaks on a 360px-wide Android screen is a failed layout. Webflow gives you two layout tools, **Flexbox** and **Grid**, and a set of **breakpoints** to adjust the design for smaller screens.
The same web page shown on a laptop, tablet and phone
One design, adjusted at each breakpoint so it reads well on every screen.
Flexbox: one direction at a time

Set an element's display to **Flex** and its children line up in a row or a column. You control direction (horizontal or vertical), alignment (start, centre, end, stretch), justification (space between, centre and so on), wrapping, and the **gap** between children. Flexbox is ideal for navigation bars, button groups, a row of icons, or a card whose button should sit at the bottom.
Grid: rows and columns together

Set display to **Grid** when you need control in two directions at once: a three-column services area, a photo gallery, or a layout where one item spans two columns. In Webflow you set the number of columns and rows, their sizes in fr units (fractions of the free space), and the gaps. Children can be placed automatically or positioned manually on specific cells.

How Webflow breakpoints cascade

Webflow's main breakpoint is **Desktop**, and that is where you design first. Styles set on Desktop cascade **down** to Tablet (991px and below), Mobile landscape (767px and below) and Mobile portrait (478px and below). A change made on Tablet affects Tablet and the smaller sizes, but never Desktop. Optional larger breakpoints (1280px, 1440px and 1920px) cascade **up** from Desktop. So the rule is: set the general style on Desktop, then override only what must change on smaller screens.
Worked example: a services grid from desktop to phone
For example, Zainab is building a catering company site. The services section has six cards in a container of max width 1140px, with a 24px gap.
Desktop: grid with 3 equal columns (1fr 1fr 1fr). Card width = (1140 - 2 x 24) / 3 = 1092 / 3 = 364px.
Tablet (991px and below): she changes the grid to 2 columns. In a 940px-wide container: (940 - 24) / 2 = 458px per card.
Mobile landscape (767px and below): she changes to 1 column, so each card fills the container width.
She reduces section padding from 96px top and bottom on Desktop to 64px on Tablet and 48px on Mobile portrait, so phone users scroll less.
She previews at 360px width and finds a heading overflowing; she lowers the H2 font size on Mobile portrait only.
Six readable cards on every screen, achieved with four overrides instead of four separate layouts.

Common phone problems and fixes

Horizontal scrolling on phones usually means one element is wider than the screen: a fixed width in px, a long word or URL, or an image without max width 100%. Set max-width instead of width, use % or rem, and check each section on Mobile portrait. Text set in vw can become tiny on phones, so give it a minimum using rem.
Navbars, images and text on small screens

Three elements cause most mobile trouble. The **Navbar** component in Webflow has a setting for the breakpoint at which the links collapse into a menu button; pick the size where the links stop fitting, usually Tablet, and style the open menu so links are large enough to tap. **Images** should sit inside wrappers with a set aspect ratio or height, and use object fit cover, so a portrait photo uploaded later does not stretch the card. **Text** needs a readable size on phones: body text around 1rem, and headings reduced step by step so a long H1 does not break into one word per line.
Tap targets: buttons and links at least about 44px tall on mobile so thumbs can hit them.
Line length: limit paragraph width on Desktop (for example max width 40rem) so lines stay comfortable to read.
Hidden elements: avoid hiding important content on mobile; if it matters on Desktop, it usually matters on a phone.

A good habit is to check all four main breakpoints after finishing each section, not at the end of the whole site. Fixing one section at a time takes minutes; fixing a whole site at the end can take days. Finally, the Webflow preview is a simulation: open the staging link on at least one real Android phone before you call a section done.

Advanced Webflow developers spend real time planning before they build. Rebuilding a section because the content did not fit is far more expensive than an hour with a notebook or a Google Doc. The plan has three parts: a **sitemap** (which pages exist), a **content model** (which content repeats and what fields it needs), and a **style guide** (the design decisions every page will reuse).

Static pages and CMS template pages

A **static page** is designed once and holds content that rarely changes: Home, About, Contact. A **Collection template page** is designed once but displays any item from a CMS Collection, so one template can produce 5 or 500 pages, each with its own address such as /projects/lekki-duplex. When you draw the sitemap, mark which is which. If a client says 'we will add a new one every month', that content belongs in the CMS.

Images in a CSV must be public URLs. Test with five rows first, check the template pages, then import the rest. You can also export a Collection to CSV as a backup.

Interactions with a purpose

Webflow's Interactions panel connects a **trigger** (mouse click, hover, an element scrolling into view, page load or page scroll) to **actions** such as move, fade (opacity), scale or show and hide. Good uses: a mobile menu opening, an FAQ answer expanding, a gentle fade-in of cards as they scroll into view. Poor uses: long animations that delay reading, text that only appears after hovering (phones cannot hover), or heavy effects that slow cheaper phones. Keep most animations short, around 0.2 to 0.5 seconds, and make sure content is readable even if an animation does not run.
Forms that work and respect privacy
Use Webflow's form block; submissions appear in the site's Forms settings and can be emailed to the client.
Give every field a visible label, not only placeholder text, and mark which fields are required.
Turn on reCAPTCHA in the form settings to reduce spam.

Collect only what you need. If the form asks for names, phone numbers or emails, add a short privacy note and a link to a privacy policy. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data; the client should take advice on their obligations.

Speed checks

Run the staging link through **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev), which uses Google's Lighthouse. Look at the mobile result first. The most common Webflow speed problem is oversized images: a 5MB photo straight from a phone. Resize images before upload (a hero rarely needs to be wider than about 2000px), use modern formats such as WebP, which Webflow can convert in the Assets panel, and keep images below the first screen on lazy loading. Avoid many large custom fonts and heavy third-party scripts.

For example, Ifeoma's home page loads slowly on mobile. PageSpeed Insights flags 6 images totalling about 14MB.
She resizes the hero from 6000px wide to 2000px and converts it to WebP: from about 5MB to about 300KB.

New total for images: 0.3 + 0.6 = 0.9MB, against 14MB before, a saving of about 13.1MB, roughly 94 percent.
She sets the card images to lazy load and keeps the hero image on eager load.
She re-runs PageSpeed Insights and records the before and after scores in her QA sheet.

One H1 per page and headings in order, without skipping levels for looks.
Every interactive element reachable and visible with the keyboard: press Tab through the page and watch the focus outline.
Use Webflow's Audit panel to catch missing alt text and other flagged issues.

Search engines read the page title, the headings and the text, so a services page titled 'Services' tells them little, while 'Event Catering in Abuja | Ada's Kitchen' says what the business does and where. Keep slugs short and readable, such as /services/wedding-catering, and decide them before launch, because changing a slug later breaks shared links unless you add a redirect.

Scope control without conflict

Change requests are normal. The aim is not to refuse them but to make their cost visible. When the client asks for something outside the proposal, reply warmly, confirm what they want, and send a short **change order**: what will be added, the extra price, and how the timeline moves. Work starts when they approve it. Keeping a simple log of requests in Google Sheets helps you see when small favours have added up to days of unpaid work.
Payment safety

Take a deposit before starting and keep the site on your workspace, or unpublished from the client's domain, until the final milestone is paid; then transfer it. Confirm payments in your actual bank or Paystack dashboard, not from a screenshot, because fake transfer alerts and edited receipts are a known scam.
Setting your hourly rate

Work out the rate rather than copying someone else's. Add up your monthly business and living costs that work must cover, then divide by the hours you can realistically bill. For example, if you need 400,000 naira a month (illustrative) and can bill 80 hours (many freelancers bill only about half their working hours, because the rest goes to sales, admin and learning), your floor rate is 400,000 / 80 = 5,000 naira an hour. Then compare it with what your niche will pay and the value of the result. For clients abroad paying in dollars, research rates on the platforms you use and remember that platform fees and transfer costs reduce what you receive.
Put it in writing

Even a simple agreement helps: the proposal plus a short contract covering payment terms, ownership transfer after final payment, how many revisions are included, what happens if the client delays content for more than a set number of weeks, and that you may show the work in your portfolio.
Care plans after launch

Many clients want help after launch but not a full project. Offer an optional monthly care plan: for example, a set number of small edits, a monthly speed and form check, and priority response. Price it from the hours it really takes. It gives the client peace of mind and gives you steadier income between projects.

The platform
Three parts you will use every day
Visual workspace in a desktop browser. It writes real HTML and CSS. Plan to work on a laptop.
Collections for repeating content, like blog posts or team members. Clients add items safely.
Free staging on webflow.io. A real domain needs a paid Site plan.

In Webflow you design visually, but the result is real HTML, CSS and JavaScript. When you add padding, Webflow writes the CSS rule. So you must understand the building blocks. You work in the Designer, on a laptop.
The CMS holds Collections, for content that repeats in the same shape, such as blog posts. Clients can add items without touching your design.
And Webflow hosts the site. Every project gets a free webflow.io address, but a real domain needs a paid Site plan.
Money safety
Plans and dollar billing
Workspace plan for you; Site plan for each site
Client pays their own Site plan
Check webflow.com/pricing the day you quote
Confirm a card that can pay in dollars
Never pay client hosting without a written deal

Webflow charges two ways. A Workspace plan is for you, the builder. A Site plan is for each live website. Usually the client pays their own Site plan, so the website is legally and financially theirs.
Prices are in US dollars and change, so check the pricing page on the day you quote. Many Nigerian bank cards limit foreign spending, so confirm a card that can pay before you promise a launch date.
And never pay a client's hosting with your own card without a written agreement on repayment.
Worked example
Three enquiries, three honest answers
Law firm, news section: Webflow with CMS
Shoe seller, naira checkout: refer to WordPress
Church event page in four days: Webflow
For example, Amaka is a Webflow freelancer in Port Harcourt. One week, three enquiries arrive on WhatsApp.
A law firm wants five pages and a news section partners can update. No payments needed. Webflow with one CMS Collection fits.

A shoe seller wants naira card checkout. Webflow Ecommerce uses Stripe and PayPal, and Stripe does not list Nigeria. So Amaka refers her to a WordPress developer and offers to design the landing page only.
A church needs one event page with a form in four days. That is a quick Webflow job. Two paid projects, one referral, and no promise she could not keep.
The box model
Why Tolu's cards did not fit
Border-box: width includes padding and border. 940px fits in 960px.
Every box: content, padding, border, margin
Card: 300px wide, 24px padding, 1px border
Three cards, two 20px gaps: 1,090px. Too wide!
Border-box: 300 x 3 + 40 = 940px. It fits
Every element is a box with four layers: the content, then padding inside the edge, then the border, then margin outside, pushing other boxes away.
For example, Tolu sets a service card 300px wide, with 24px padding each side and a 1px border.
With content-box sizing, width means content only. So each card is really 350px.
Three cards and two 20px gaps make 1,090px. That overflows her 960px container.
Webflow's default is border-box, where width includes padding and border. Then the row is 940px and fits. An old code embed had changed it. She removed it, and the row fits.
Clean structure
How a professional page nests
Section: one band, padding and background
Content: real headings, text, images
Classes named by meaning, e.g. services_card
Open the Navigator panel. You want a tidy tree, not a pile of unnamed Div Blocks. Each band of the page is a Section.
Inside it, a Container sets a maximum width, for example 1200px, and centres it.
A layout wrapper decides how children sit: side by side, in a grid, or stacked.
Then the content. Use real headings in order, not paragraphs made big.
Style with classes, reusable named styles. A combo class, like button plus is-secondary, adds a variation. And name things by meaning. Div Block 47 tells nobody anything.
Layout tools
Use Flexbox for a line of things, like a navigation bar or a row of buttons.
Use Grid when you need rows and columns together, like a three-column services area. Columns are sized in fr, a fraction of the free space.
Breakpoints
Zainab's services grid, desktop to phone
Set styles on Desktop. Override only what must change below.
Desktop: 3 columns, 364px cards
Tablet, 991px and below: 2 columns
Mobile landscape, 767px and below: 1 column
Section padding: 96px, then 64px, then 48px
Test at 360px and on a real Android phone
Most visitors arrive on a phone. In Webflow you design on Desktop, and styles cascade down to smaller screens.
For example, Zainab builds a catering site with six service cards. On Desktop, 3 columns, so each card is 364px.
On Tablet she changes the grid to 2 columns.
On Mobile landscape, 1 column, so each card fills the width.
She reduces section padding so phone users scroll less.
Then she previews at 360px and finds a heading overflowing, so she lowers it on Mobile portrait only. Four overrides, not four separate layouts. And always open the link on a real phone.
Key points
Remember
Webflow builds real HTML and CSS
Ask about payments first; refer when it's wrong
Border-box keeps width arithmetic simple
Section, Container, wrapper, content
Design on Desktop, override below, test on a phone

To remember. Ask about payments and editing needs first. Know your box model. Keep a clean structure with meaningful class names. And design on Desktop, override only what must change, and check every section on a real phone.

Plan before you build
A build plan has three parts
Which pages exist. Mark static pages and CMS template pages.
Which content repeats, and the fields each Collection needs.
A hidden page of headings, buttons and colours, stored as Variables.

Rebuilding a section because the content did not fit costs far more than an hour of planning. First, the sitemap. A static page, like About, is designed once. A template page is designed once but shows any item from a Collection.
Second, the content model. If the client says, we will add a new one every month, that content belongs in the CMS, with the right fields.
Third, a style guide page. Store colours and sizes as Variables, so when the brand colour changes, you change one variable and the whole site updates.
Worked example
Planning an interior design studio site
Static pages: Home, About, Services, Contact
Collections: Projects and Testimonials
Option field for project type; switch for Featured
4 static + 1 template = 5 designs to build
For example, Funmi runs an interior design studio in Abuja and adds about two projects a month. She needs 4 static pages.
Projects repeat monthly, so they become a Collection. Testimonials too, linked to projects with a reference field. Plan references early, because they are harder to add later.
Project type is an Option field, so Residential never becomes residental. Featured is a yes or no switch.
That is 5 designs to build, even if the site grows to 50 project pages. Get the client to approve this plan. It becomes your baseline for scope.
Step by step
From Collection to live pages
Test like a client: a very long title, and an item with no image.
Create the Collection and add your fields
Write help text, e.g. landscape, 1600px wide
Add three to five real items
Connect the template page to the fields
Add a Collection List to Home
Filter, sort and limit, e.g. latest 3 featured
Create the Collection, for example Projects, and add the fields from your plan.
Write help text on every field, so the client knows exactly what to upload.
Add a few real items, so you design with true content lengths.
On the template page, connect each element to a field. The heading shows the project name, the image shows the cover.
On Home, add a Collection List, filter to Featured, sort newest first, and limit it to 3. Conditional visibility hides a button when its field is empty, instead of showing a broken link.
Then open Editor mode and act like the client. Add a very long title and an item with no image. Fix what breaks now, because the client will do exactly this in the first month.
Interactions
Movement with a purpose
Good uses
Mobile menu opening
FAQ answer expanding
Short fade-in, 0.2 to 0.5 seconds
Poor uses
Long animations that delay reading
Text shown only on hover
Heavy effects on cheaper phones
An interaction joins a trigger, like a click or scroll, to an action, like a fade. Good uses help people: a menu opening, an FAQ expanding, a short fade-in.
Poor uses get in the way. Phones cannot hover, so never hide text behind a hover. And content must be readable even if an animation does not run.
Privacy
A visible label on every field
reCAPTCHA on to reduce spam
Collect only what you need
A privacy note and policy link
Test on the live domain; client gets the email

Give every field a visible label, and turn on reCAPTCHA. Collect only what you need. If you ask for names, phone numbers or emails, add a privacy note and a policy link. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties here, so the client should take advice.
Then test every form on the live domain, and confirm the client actually receives the email.
Speed
Ifeoma cuts her page weight
Under 1MB of images instead of 14MB matters when data is expensive.
PageSpeed Insights flags 6 images, about 14MB
Hero: 6000px to 2000px, WebP, about 300KB
5 card photos: 1000px wide, about 600KB
Lazy load the cards; re-run the test
The most common Webflow speed problem is oversized photos straight from a phone. For example, Ifeoma's home page has 6 images totalling about 14MB.
She resizes the hero to 2000px wide and converts it to WebP. About 5MB becomes about 300KB.
The card photos go from about 9MB to about 600KB.
She sets them to lazy load and tests again. A saving of roughly 94 percent, and that matters a great deal to a visitor on mobile data.
Before launch
Accessibility, search and domain
Contrast at least 4.5:1 for normal text
Alt text on meaningful images; one H1
Tab through the page and see the focus
Clear titles, e.g. Event Catering in Abuja
301 redirects, DNS records, SSL on
Check colour contrast before you build.
Add alt text to meaningful images, use one H1 per page, and keep headings in order.
Press Tab through every page and watch the focus outline.
A page titled Services tells search engines little. Event Catering in Abuja says what and where.
Add redirects for old addresses, copy Webflow's DNS records into your registrar, keep SSL on, and test again on the live domain.
Key points
Remember
Sitemap, content model and style guide first
Repeating content belongs in the CMS
Help text and Option fields keep it client-proof
Resize images; check contrast and keyboard
Forms: minimal data, privacy note, live test

To remember. Plan before you build, and get the plan approved. Put repeating content in the CMS and make it client-proof. Keep pages light for mobile data, accessible, and clearly titled. And test forms and the domain live before you say the site is done.

Discovery
Five areas for every discovery call
Goal: what should a visitor do?
Audience: who visits, on what device?
Content: text, photos and logo ready?
Updates: what will they change, how often?
Budget and timeline: any fixed launch date?
Most failed website projects fail before the first pixel. The developer built what they assumed, not what the business needed. So start with a 30 to 45 minute discovery call.
Goal. Turn wishes into one measurable goal, for example enquiries rising from about 5 a month to 15.
Audience. Who visits, and on what device.
Content. Is the text, photos and logo ready, and who writes new content?
Updates. What they will change often becomes a CMS Collection.
Budget and timeline. And ask who owns the domain and can log in. Lost domain logins often delay launches.
Worked example
Grace works backwards from 10 weeks
Never collect passwords over chat. Ask to be invited instead.
Goal: enquiries from about 8 to 20 a month
1 week to plan
4 weeks to build
1 week content entry, 1 week testing and training
3 weeks of buffer for late content
For example, Grace meets a private primary school in Ibadan. Admissions open in 10 weeks. The school gets about 8 enquiries a month, and wants 20.
She works backwards from the date. 1 week to plan.
4 weeks to build.
1 week for content entry, and 1 for testing and training.
That leaves 3 weeks of buffer, because photos and text often arrive late. Within 48 hours she sends a one-page brief for approval.
Never ask a client to send passwords in a WhatsApp group or email. Ask them to invite you as a collaborator, and remove your access after handoff.
Pricing
Pricing the school website
For example, Grace prices the school site. These naira figures are illustrative only.
70 hours x 8,000 per hour
10% buffer for content delays
Illustrative only. Set your own rate.
Grace estimates each task from her own records: 5 static pages, 2 templates, 2 Collections, forms, testing and training. That is 58 hours.
She adds 20 percent for project management and revisions, about 12 hours, making 70.
At an illustrative 8,000 naira an hour, that is 560,000 naira.
She adds a 10 percent buffer for content delays.

Milestones
Get paid in three stages
248,000 naira before any work starts.
248,000 naira when the home page and template are approved.
124,000 naira before the site goes on the client's domain.
Split the price into milestones. 40 percent deposit, 248,000 naira, before you start.
40 percent more when the home page and template design are approved.
And the last 20 percent, 124,000, before publishing to the custom domain. Together, 620,000.
The proposal
Say what the price buys
5 page designs
News and Events Collections
Enquiry form, all breakpoints
1-hour Editor training
Copywriting and photography
Logo design
Online payments
Ongoing updates after launch
A fixed price only protects you if the scope is written clearly. List what is included.

Then list what is not included. Exclusions prevent most disputes. When the client asks for something new, reply warmly and send a short change order: what is added, the extra price, and how the timeline moves.
Protect your money
Take a deposit before starting
Keep the site on your workspace until paid
Confirm in your bank or Paystack dashboard
Never trust a screenshot of a transfer
Take a deposit before you start. Keep the site on your own workspace, or off the client's domain, until the final milestone is paid.
Confirm every payment in your actual bank or Paystack dashboard. Fake transfer alerts and edited receipts are a known scam.
Handoff
Finish so the client owns it
Confirm the final payment
Transfer the site to the client
Record a short how-to video
Train live: the client does each task
Send a handoff document; remove your access
A project is finished when the client owns the site, can update it, and would recommend you. Confirm final payment, then transfer the site.
Record a short video on adding a CMS item, and train live while the client does each task. That happy moment is the best time to ask for a testimonial.
Leave a handoff document, and remove any access you no longer need. Later, with permission, write an honest case study using only verified results.
Key points
Remember
One measurable goal and a signed brief
Price from hours, rate and a buffer
Milestones; confirm payments in your dashboard
Exclusions and change orders protect scope
Choose a niche; track outreach every week

To remember. Get a signed brief with one measurable goal. Build your price from real hours, and be paid in milestones. Write exclusions and use change orders. Then choose a niche, like schools or clinics, and track your outreach every Friday for 90 days.
